newsitem.title: USA: Fran swirls nearer South Carolina coast.
newsitem.headline: Fran swirls nearer South Carolina coast.

text.p: Hurricane Fran bore down on the South Carolina coast on Thursday, forcing hundreds of thousands of residents to seek refuge inland and rekindling memories of the devastation of Hurricane Hugo.

The National Hurricane Centre predicted Fran's most likely target would be the coastline between 300-year-old Charleston, a city battered seven years ago by deadly Hurricane Hugo, and the Myrtle Beach resort area.

Gale-force winds surrounding the broad storm were expected to begin lashing the coastline by early afternoon. The full brunt of Fran's 115 mph winds (185 kmh) were predicted to make landfall late on Thursday evening.

Forecasters said Fran would dump up to 10 inches (25 cms) of rain in its path, flooding coastal neighbourhoods and inland areas that were still soaked from recent heavy rains. Dangerous storm surges of more than 10 feet (3 meters) were also expected.
"Once Fran comes, it may be around until dawn tomorrow," said Dennis Clark, emergency operations centre director in Charleston.

Hundreds of thousands of residents living along the South Carolina coast fled inland after boarding up windows and gathering hurricane supplies. Officials said at least 175,000 residents and tourists were evacuated from Georgetown and Beaufort counties, an area that did not include the popular Myrtle Beach resorts.
Emergency officials enforced mandatory evacuations of beachfront properties in South Carolina. Officials knocked on resident's doors to move out any stragglers wanting to stay.
Nursing homes took the elderly to shelters or called relatives to collect them and emergency teams worked overnight to pull down roadside billboards.
Hurricane warnings for Fran stretched across the coastline of four states early on Thursday, from Georgia, through to the Carolinas and Virginia.
At 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), the centre of Fran was about 215 miles (345 km) southeast of Charleston and was moving north-northwest.
Gale-force winds were expected to begin slapping the coastline at lunchtime, and the hurricane-force winds that extend outward up to 145 miles (230 km) could strike by late evening.

Fran picked up a little speed during the night and was moving north-northwest at 14 mph (22 kmh). Forecasters said they were concerned that Fran could strengthen as it moved over the warm Gulf Stream waters off the coast.

For many Charleston residents, the storm was a frightening reminder of Hurricane Hugo, which ravaged the historic city Sept. 21, 1989, with winds of more than 140 mph (225 kph). That hurricane killed 27, destroyed 17,000 homes and caused more than $7 billion in damage.
More than a dozen schools were turned into shelters in the Charleston area, officials said.
Coastal roads from Georgia to North Carolina were clogged on Wednesday when residents, visitors, and sun worshippers taking in the last bit of summer at the beach had to flee.
Bumper-to-bumper traffic streamed out of Charleston, a preserved city of antebellum plantations, stunning gardens, open markets, and host of the famous Spoleto arts festival.
Residents and merchants locked shutters over windows and nailed plywood on others. Gasoline stations were jammed with long lines of motorists anxious to fill up their cars before the storm hit.
"The people of Charleston learned a lot from Hugo," said Charleston Mayor Joe Riley.
South Carolina Gov. David Beasley declared a statewide state of emergency early on Wednesday and called for evacuation of beachfront property in six counties.
Georgia Gov. Zell Miller declared a state of emergency in 11 counties along the coast and urged voluntary evacuations. It was mandatory for those on barrier islands.
Further north, emergency management officials worried about the dangerous strength of Fran, evacuated residents of Ocracoke Island, North Carolina.

Peter Stone, emergency management manager for the island that dots North Carolina's famed Outer Banks, said the decision was based on the proximity and strength of the storm. "It was time to get everybody the hell out of here," he said.

At Cape Canaveral, about halfway up the Florida coast, NASA rolled the space shuttle Atlantis back to its massive garage as a precaution against storm conditions, delaying its takeoff. Atlantis, already six weeks late, had been due to blast off on Sept. 14 on a mission to pick up U.S. astronaut Shannon Lucid from the Russian Mir space station and drop off her replacement, John Blaha.
